articles.title: Expressing Breast Milk: Hand Expression
articles.summary: How to express breast milk by hand, no pump needed
articles.quickTake: Hand expression needs no pump or power. Make a "C" with your thumb and fingers, press back towards your chest, then compress and release in a steady rhythm. It should never hurt.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Why hand express?

items.title: No equipment
items.text: No pump, electricity or special equipment needed

items.title: Handy when it counts
items.text: Useful for colostrum, engorgement, painful nipples, or when a pump isn't available

items.title: Helps supply and latch
items.text: Can help stimulate milk production and may soften the breast for attachment

sections.content: How to hand express

items.title: Position
items.text: Thumb above and fingers below the nipple, 1–2 inches behind the nipple, to form a "C".

image.alt: Hand forming a C shape around the breast, thumb above and fingers below the nipple

items.title: Press
items.text: Gently press back towards the chest.

image.alt: Close-up of thumb pressing gently behind the nipple with drops of milk

items.title: Compress & release
items.text: Bring your fingers together: press, compress, release. Repeat rhythmically and move around the breast.

image.alt: Milk being hand expressed into a clean glass cup

sections.title: Helpful tips
items: Warmth, gentle massage and relaxation may help milk flow
Think about or look at your baby to encourage let-down

sections.title: Be gentle
sections.content: Do not squeeze hard or pull the nipple. Hand expression should not hurt.
Watch how it's done

articles.title: Why is breastfeeding so good for your baby?
articles.summary: How breastmilk is made for your baby and why it matters
articles.quickTake: Breastmilk gives your baby all the nutrients, calories and fluids they need, helps build immunity, and even changes to match your baby as they grow.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Human milk is uniquely designed for babies, providing all the nutrients, calories, and fluids needed for their health.

items.title: Brain and growth
items.text: Supports your baby's brain development and growth

items.title: Easy to digest
items.text: Gentle on your baby's tummy

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.text: Shares antibodies and other protective factors from mother to baby

sections.content: Lower risk of illness

items: Lower risk of asthma, obesity, type 1 diabetes, childhood leukemia, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)
Breastfed babies are less likely to have ear infections and stomach bugs

sections.title: Tailor-made for your baby
sections.content: Breastmilk composition changes with your baby's growth and nutritional needs: premature vs full-term, boy vs girl, time of day (morning vs night), and even within a feed (foremilk vs hindmilk).

articles.title: What's inside breastmilk?
articles.summary: The nutrients, living cells and protective factors in breastmilk
articles.quickTake: Breastmilk is more than food. Alongside fat, protein and carbohydrate, it carries living cells, antibodies, hormones and prebiotics that protect your baby and support healthy development.
articles.author: NariCare Team

items.title: Macronutrients
items.text: Fat, protein, and carbohydrate

items.title: Micronutrients
items.text: Vitamins and minerals

sections.content: Breastmilk is packed with components that actively protect your baby and support healthy development.

items.title: Living cells
items.text: Breastmilk carries immune cells such as white blood cells (leukocytes) and stem cells. Colostrum, the first milk, is especially rich in these cells, giving extra protection in the early days.

items.title: Antibodies
items.text: Breastmilk is full of antibodies that help protect your baby from germs.

items.title: Protective proteins
items.text: Proteins like lactoferrin and lysozyme help fight bacteria and viruses.

items.title: Hormones and cytokines
items.text: Tiny messengers that support growth, guide metabolism, and strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Growth factors
items.text: Help your baby's body develop: support a healthy gut, help blood vessels form, and play a role in brain and hormone development.

items.title: Human Milk Oligosaccharides
items.text: Act as prebiotics, encouraging the growth of beneficial bacteria (probiotics) in your baby's gut.

sections.content: Watch: a drop of breastmilk under a microscope

media.title: A drop of breastmilk under a microscope

articles.title: Difference between breastmilk and formula
articles.summary: What formula is missing compared to breastmilk
articles.quickTake: Compared to breastmilk, formula is missing many things babies need to be strong and healthy. Formula-fed babies and children have a higher risk of several illnesses.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Compared to breastmilk, formula is missing many things babies need to be strong, healthy and smart.
Did you know?
Formula-fed babies have a greater risk of:

items: Ear infections
Diarrhea and constipation
Pneumonia
SIDS (Sudden Infant Death Syndrome)

sections.content: Children who are formula-fed have a greater risk of:

items: Obesity (becoming overweight)
Diabetes
Asthma and allergies
Cancer

sections.title: Breastmilk has more of the good things babies need
sections.content: Living cells, antibodies, protective proteins and prebiotics in breastmilk cannot be copied by formula.

articles.title: Benefits of breastfeeding for your baby
articles.summary: Head-to-toe health benefits of breastfeeding for your baby
articles.quickTake: The longer a baby is breastfed, the lower the risk of nearly every serious childhood illness. The benefits reach from brain and eyes to heart, gut, immunity and skin.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: The incidence of nearly every serious disease you don't want your child to get is lower the longer a baby is breastfed. From head to toe, a breastfed baby enjoys smarter brains, clearer vision, better dental alignment, healthier hearts, good gut health, fewer cancers, a lower risk of SIDS, and much more.
Breastfeeding benefits from top to bottom

items.title: Brain
items.text: Higher IQ in breastfed children. Cholesterol and other fats in human milk support the growth of nerve tissue.

items.title: Eyes
items.text: Visual acuity is higher in babies fed human milk.

items.title: Ears
items.text: Breastfed babies get fewer ear infections.

items.title: Mouth
items.text: Less need for orthodontics in children breastfed more than a year, and better muscle development of the face from suckling.

items.title: Throat
items.text: Breastfed children are less likely to need tonsillectomies.

items.title: Breathing
items.text: Fewer and less severe upper respiratory infections, less wheezing, less pneumonia and less influenza.

items.title: Heart
items.text: May have lower cholesterol as adults. Heart rates are lower in breastfed infants.

items.title: Digestion
items.text: Less diarrhea and fewer gut infections. Six months of exclusive breastfeeding lowers the risk of food allergies, and of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis in adulthood.

items.title: Immune system
items.text: Better response to vaccinations, a more mature immune system, and a lower risk of childhood cancer.

items.title: Hormones
items.text: Reduced risk of getting diabetes.

items.title: Kidneys
items.text: With less salt and protein, human milk is easier on a baby's kidneys.

items.title: Joints and muscles
items.text: Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis is less common in breastfed children.

items.title: Skin
items.text: Less allergic eczema in breastfed infants.

items.title: Growth
items.text: Leaner at one year and less likely to be obese later in life.

sections.content: Also

items: Appendix: children with acute appendicitis are less likely to have been breastfed
Urinary tract: fewer infections in breastfed infants
Bowels: less constipation, and stools of breastfed babies have a less offensive odor

articles.title: Benefits of breastfeeding for the mother
articles.summary: How breastfeeding supports your own health
articles.quickTake: Breastfeeding is healthier for mothers too: faster recovery, lower risk of breast, uterine and ovarian cancer, stronger bones, less postpartum anxiety, and lower cost than formula.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Besides being healthier for babies, breastfeeding is healthier for mothers: faster postpartum recovery and pregnancy weight loss, stronger mother-infant bonding, lower cancer risk, less osteoporosis, natural child spacing, and lower cost than formula feeding.

items.title: Reduces the risk of breast cancer
items.text: Women who breastfeed reduce their risk of developing breast cancer by as much as 25 percent.

items.title: Reduces the risk of uterine and ovarian cancer
items.text: One reason for the cancer-fighting effect is that estrogen levels are lower during lactation.

items.title: Lessens osteoporosis
items.text: Non-breastfeeding women have a four times greater chance of developing osteoporosis and are more likely to suffer hip fractures after menopause.

items.title: Benefits child spacing
items.text: Breastfeeding delays ovulation, so the longer you breastfeed, the more you can practice natural child spacing if you wish.

items.title: Less postpartum anxiety and depression
items.text: Studies show breastfeeding mothers have less postpartum anxiety and depression than formula-feeding mothers.

items.title: Promotes postpartum weight loss
items.text: Breastfeeding mothers show larger reductions in hip size and more fat loss by one month postpartum, and tend to return to their pre-pregnancy weight sooner.

items.title: Costs less
items.text: Breastfeeding saves the cost of formula and feeding supplies.

articles.title: Global recommendations for breastfeeding
articles.summary: What global health guidance recommends for breastfeeding
articles.quickTake: Start breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, breastfeed exclusively for 6 months, then add other foods while continuing to breastfeed for up to two years or beyond.
articles.author: NariCare Team

items.title: Within the first hour
items.text: Initiate breastfeeding within the first hour of birth.

items.title: First 6 months
items.text: Exclusively breastfeed for the first 6 months of life, meaning no other foods or liquids, including water.

items.title: From 6 months
items.text: Introduce complementary foods while continuing to breastfeed for up to two years of age or beyond.

articles.title: Do you actually have a low milk supply?
articles.summary: The reliable signs of enough milk, and what does not mean low supply
articles.quickTake: If your baby is gaining weight well on breastmilk alone and has enough wet and dirty diapers, your supply is likely fine. How your breasts feel, fussiness and pumping output are not reliable signs.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.title: The reliable signs
sections.content: If your baby is gaining weight well on breastmilk alone and has an adequate number of wet and dirty diapers, your milk supply is likely adequate.
Breast feel, baby's behaviour, feeding frequency, let-down sensation, and pumping output are not reliable measures of milk supply.
These do NOT necessarily mean low milk supply

items: Baby feeds frequently or wants frequent contact
Baby suddenly feeds more often or for longer, often a growth spurt
Baby feeds more frequently or is fussy in the evening
Baby feeds for shorter periods as they become more efficient
Baby is fussy
Baby readily takes a bottle after breastfeeding
Breasts leak less, stop leaking, or feel softer
You do not feel the let-down or it feels different
You pump little or no milk: pumping output does not accurately reflect milk supply

articles.title: Is your baby getting enough milk?
articles.summary: Weight gain and diaper counts to check by age
articles.quickTake: Weight gain and diapers tell you most. After the first few days, expect 6 or more wet diapers a day, steady weight gain, and a baby who is alert and content after feeds.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Birth to 6 weeks

rows: 5–7% loss is normal in the first 3–4 days. Back to birth weight by 2 weeks. 142–198 g/week once milk comes in.
Day 1: 1, Day 2: 2, Day 3: 3, Day 4+: 6 or more a day. By Day 7: 5–6+ very wet a day. Urine pale and mild-smelling.
3–4 or more a day by Day 4. Yellow and loose by Day 5.

sections.content: After 6 weeks

rows: 0–4 months: 142–198 g/week. 4–6 months: 113–142 g/week. 6–12 months: 57–113 g/week.
4–5 or more very wet a day (often wetter in the morning). Pale, mild-smelling urine.
Varies widely, from several a day to 1 every 7–10+ days. Normal if stools stay soft and weight gain is steady.

sections.title: Other positive signs
items: Breasts feel softer after feeding
Baby is alert, active, and content after feeds
Baby is hitting developmental milestones

articles.title: How to increase your milk supply?
articles.summary: Why supply drops and what helps it grow
articles.quickTake: Milk works on supply and demand: the more often and more effectively milk is removed, the more you make. Frequent feeds, a good latch and less unnecessary bottle use all help.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.title: The key principle
sections.content: Milk production is a supply-and-demand process. Frequent and effective milk removal leads to increased milk production.
What can reduce milk supply?

items: Infrequent or ineffective milk removal: poor positioning or attachment, sleepy or inefficient feeding, or stopping feeds too early
Supplements, bottles or pacifiers that reduce time or stimulation at the breast
Scheduled feeds rather than feeding according to baby's cues
Nipple shields or other factors that interfere with milk transfer
Infant factors such as jaundice, tongue-tie or other health or anatomical problems
Maternal factors such as postpartum haemorrhage, retained placenta, anaemia, thyroid or hormonal problems, previous breast surgery or injury, medications or smoking

sections.content: To increase milk supply

items.title: Get the latch right
items.text: Ensure effective positioning, attachment and milk transfer.

items.title: Feed often
items.text: Breastfeed frequently and while baby is actively feeding; offer both breasts.

items.title: Use breast compression
items.text: Use breast compression or switch nursing when helpful.

items.title: Express if needed
items.text: If baby is not transferring milk effectively, express after or between feeds to maintain and increase milk production.

items.title: Limit unnecessary bottles
items.text: Reduce unnecessary bottles and pacifiers and address supplementation when possible. If supplementation is medically necessary, expressed breastmilk is preferred when available.

items.title: Look after yourself
items.text: Rest, eat well, and drink according to thirst.

sections.title: If baby is not gaining weight
sections.content: If your baby is not gaining weight or is losing weight, seek help from your baby's pediatrician and a lactation consultant. Supplementation may be medically necessary while milk supply is being addressed.

articles.title: Sore nipples
articles.summary: Common causes of nipple pain and what helps
articles.quickTake: Mild tenderness in the early days is common, but severe, cracked or bleeding nipples usually point to a cause, most often a shallow latch. A better latch and position usually help.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Mild tenderness is common in the early days of breastfeeding, but persistent, severe, cracked, or bleeding nipples may indicate an underlying problem.
Common causes

items: Shallow or painful latch, the most common cause: baby isn't taking in enough areola and is sucking only on the nipple
Tongue-tie or high palate
Flat or inverted nipples making it difficult to attach
Breast pump use: incorrect flange fit or too much suction
Other causes: dermatitis, infection, white spots or blisters, or nipple vasospasm

sections.content: What can help?

items.title: Check the latch
items.text: Check and improve baby's attachment and positioning, and try different positions.

items.title: Start on the less sore side
items.text: Nurse on the least sore side until let-down, then gently switch baby to the other breast.

items.title: Re-latch if it hurts
items.text: If breastfeeding remains painful, break the suction and re-latch.

items.title: Soothe the skin
items.text: Nipple creams or ointments can help healing. Avoid soaps and other irritants on the nipple area.

sections.title: Pain that doesn't settle
sections.content: Seek support from a lactation consultant if pain persists.

articles.title: Engorgement
articles.summary: Why breasts get hard and swollen, and how to ease it
articles.quickTake: Engorgement is hard, swollen, tender breasts as your milk increases, usually on days 2–5. Frequent feeding, brief warmth before feeds, cool packs between feeds and gentle expression help.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Hard, swollen and tender breasts caused by an increase in milk, blood and other fluids as milk supply increases.
Signs

items: Usually affects both breasts at the same time
Breasts feel hard, heavy, warm, swollen and tender
Commonly occurs when milk is "coming in", usually day 2–5 after birth
May involve the whole breast, including towards the armpit
Milk may not flow easily
Nipples or areola may become stretched or flattened, making it harder for baby to attach

sections.content: Common causes

items: Milk supply increasing after birth
Baby going longer between feeds
Baby sleeping for longer stretches
Breasts becoming very full, especially overnight
Can also happen later if baby suddenly feeds less, sleeps longer or weans quickly

sections.content: What can help?

items.title: Feed often
items.text: Breastfeed frequently, according to baby's needs. If breasts become very full and uncomfortable, wake baby for a feed, especially at night.

items.title: Before feeding
items.text: Loosen or remove your bra and use brief gentle warmth, or lightly stroke the breast towards the nipple to help milk flow.

items.title: Between feeds
items.text: Use cool packs to reduce swelling and inflammation.

items.title: Express a little
items.text: If still uncomfortably full, hand express only until comfortable.

items.title: Soften the areola
items.text: If the areola is swollen and the nipple flattened, use reverse pressure softening to soften the area and help baby attach.

sections.title: If it isn't improving
sections.content: Discuss pain relief or anti-inflammatory medication with your gynecologist. If engorgement is not improving, seek help from a lactation consultant.

sections.title: In short
sections.content: Engorgement is generalised breast fullness, swelling and tenderness, usually affecting both breasts.

articles.title: Blocked duct
articles.summary: What a blocked duct is and how to manage it gently
articles.quickTake: A "blocked duct" is a sore, firm or lumpy area caused by inflammation, not something that needs to be pushed out. Keep feeding as usual, handle the breast gently, and use cool packs between feeds.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: A sore, firm or lumpy area caused by inflammation, not usually a physical blockage inside the milk duct.
Signs

items: A single firm lump or a localised swollen or lumpy area
Redness, tenderness or pain, especially when milk starts flowing
The affected area may not soften well after feeding
Can occur anywhere in the breast, including towards the armpit

sections.content: Common causes

items: Longer gaps between feeds or baby sleeping longer
Rushed or incomplete feeds, or ineffective milk removal
Producing more milk than baby needs
Pressure on the breast from clothing or sleeping position

sections.content: What can help?

items.title: Keep feeding as usual
items.text: Continue breastfeeding according to baby's needs. There is no need to "empty" the breast.

items.title: Check the latch
items.text: Check positioning and attachment, and express if baby is not feeding effectively.

items.title: Before feeding
items.text: Relax, loosen your bra, use brief warmth, and gently stroke the breast towards the nipple. Avoid deep or aggressive massage.

items.title: Between feeds
items.text: Use cool packs for pain and inflammation.

items.title: Express a little
items.text: If still uncomfortably full, hand express only until comfortable.

items.title: Be gentle
items.text: Handle the breast gently and discuss anti-inflammatory or pain medication with your gynecologist.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.content: A "blocked duct" is localised inflammation, not something that needs to be pushed or massaged out. Early management may help prevent it progressing to mastitis.

articles.title: Mastitis
articles.summary: Signs of mastitis, how to manage it, and when to see a doctor
articles.quickTake: Mastitis is inflammation of the breast, sometimes with infection. Keep breastfeeding, use cold packs between feeds, rest, and see a doctor if you don't improve within 12–24 hours.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Inflammation of the breast tissue, which can develop from engorgement, damaged nipples, or overfull breasts. Bacterial infection may or may not be present.
Symptoms

items: Feeling unwell with fever, chills, or a fast heart rate
A swollen, hot and painful area of the breast
Skin may become red or darker, shiny, or streaked
Can develop quickly, sometimes with feeling unwell as the first sign

sections.content: Management

items.title: Keep breastfeeding
items.text: Continue breastfeeding frequently to keep milk flowing and maintain milk supply. Breastmilk remains safe for your baby during mastitis.

items.title: Check the latch
items.text: Ensure good positioning and attachment; express if baby is not breastfeeding well.

items.title: Cold between feeds
items.text: Cold packs between feeds can relieve pain and swelling.

items.title: Warmth only before feeds
items.text: Warmth may be used just before feeding to help milk flow. Avoid warmth at other times, as it may worsen inflammation.

items.title: Rest and recover
items.text: Rest, drink plenty of fluids, and eat well.

sections.title: When to seek medical help
sections.content: See a doctor if you do not improve or get worse within 12–24 hours, or sooner if you feel very unwell. Pain or inflammation medicines may be recommended, and antibiotics may be prescribed when needed; breastfeeding can continue. If not treated promptly, mastitis can occasionally lead to a breast abscess.

articles.title: Breast abscess
articles.summary: What a breast abscess is, how it is treated, and breastfeeding during treatment
articles.quickTake: A breast abscess is a pocket of pus, usually after mastitis that wasn't treated early. It is treatable by draining and antibiotics, and breastfeeding is safe and recommended during treatment.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: A breast abscess is a pocket of pus (infected fluid) in the breast, usually developing when mastitis is not treated early or does not respond to treatment. It can be painful and uncomfortable, but it is treatable and the breast can heal with appropriate care.
Treatment

items.title: Needle aspiration
items.text: Infected fluid is drained using a needle and syringe, sometimes with ultrasound guidance.

items.title: Incision and drainage
items.text: A small procedure may be needed to drain the abscess; a drain may be left in temporarily.

items.title: Antibiotics
items.text: Given to treat the infection.

sections.content: Breastfeeding during treatment

items: Continue breastfeeding if possible: breastfeeding is safe and recommended during treatment
If direct feeding is not possible, express milk from the affected breast until the drain is removed
Milk leaking from the wound does not prevent healing; breastmilk contains immune factors that support healing and help protect against infection
The breast may take some time to return to normal, but gradually heals with continued breastfeeding

articles.title: Tongue tie
articles.summary: How tongue-tie can affect breastfeeding and how it is assessed
articles.quickTake: Tongue-tie can limit how well some babies attach, causing nipple pain and poor milk transfer. Many babies with a visible frenulum feed well. Get the latch checked first, then a referral if needed.
articles.author: NariCare Team

sections.content: Tongue-tie (ankyloglossia) occurs when the lingual frenulum restricts tongue movement, which may make attachment and breastfeeding difficult for some babies. A visible frenulum does not necessarily cause feeding problems; many babies breastfeed well.
Signs breastfeeding may not be going well

items: Nipple pain or damage, including flattening, compression or stripe marks, or cracks
Poor milk transfer
Slow infant weight gain

sections.content: These signs can have causes other than tongue-tie.
Why can tongue-tie affect breastfeeding?

Restricted tongue movement may prevent the baby from taking a full mouthful of breast tissue and drawing the nipple far enough back into the mouth. This can result in "nipple-feeding", nipple damage and reduced milk transfer.
Assessment and management

items.title: Check the latch first
items.text: Positioning and attachment should be assessed first with a breastfeeding counsellor or lactation consultant.

items.title: Referral if suspected
items.text: If tongue-tie is suspected to be contributing to breastfeeding difficulties, referral to a pediatric dentist for diagnosis and possible treatment may be appropriate.

items.title: Frenulum release
items.text: If tongue-tie is confirmed to be interfering with breastfeeding, frenulum release may help.
